title.text: The Hornbills: Heralds of the Tropics

pieces.text: Found in tropical and subtropical regions of Africa and Southeast Asia, hornbills are known for their striking characteristics, from the way they look to the way they sound. These unusual birds can range from one foot to as much as five feet in length. They generally have long tails and short, thick legs. Their eyes are protected by long, wispy feathers that look almost like eyelashes. But perhaps the most striking feature of hornbills is the

that sits on top of their oversized, downward-curving bills. A casque is a usually hollow, hornlike structure thought to amplify the sound of the birds' calls so that they can be heard from farther away. The louder sounds may help hornbills attract mates. To support the weight of their bills and casques, the top two vertebrae in hornbills' necks are fused together.

textContent.text: With about sixty different species of hornbills, there are many interesting differences between varieties. One of the most stunning hornbills is the rhinoceros hornbill, the national bird of Malaysia. These hornbills have black feathers, a striped tail, and a large casque that frequently curls upward at the tip. The hornbills' casques and part of their bills are stained a vivid red-orange color. This staining occurs when the birds use their bills to preen. The birds' bodies secrete a special red-orange preening oil, and the birds use their bills to rub the oil into their feathers. Reaching up to four feet in length, rhinoceros hornbills are quite a sight! However, since these giant birds spend most of their time feasting on fruit high up in the rainforest canopy, they are more likely to be heard than seen.

Africa's southern yellow-billed hornbills are much easier to spot. They are sometimes called "flying bananas" because of the way their yellow beaks stand out from their salt-and-pepper feathers. These hornbills are about two feet long. Their casques are just small ridges along the tops of their bills. Yellow-billed hornbills feed on the ground in dry savannas, primarily eating insects and other small prey. They have an unlikely relationship with dwarf mongooses: the two go on hunting trips together. This partnership is beneficial to both animals. Mongooses stir up insects for hornbills to eat. In return, hornbills warn mongooses when predators are nearby.

Perhaps the most unusual of all the hornbills is the helmeted hornbill of Southeast Asia. Helmeted hornbills have a distinctive patch of loose, leathery, featherless skin at their throats. The skin is red in the males and turquoise in the females. It forms a pouch that the birds pack with fruit to carry back to their nests. Unlike other hornbills, helmeted hornbills have solid, bony casques that look like large red bumps on their bills. Two hornbills competing for territory sometimes take flight and clash their casques together in dramatic mid-air collisions. The casques are prized for their "red ivory," which is used to carve expensive jewelry and ornaments. In fact, the illegal red ivory trade is the main reason why this amazing bird is critically endangered.

Hornbills are spectacular birds, no matter the species. Unfortunately, their unique qualities are also one of the reasons that some hornbill species are at risk of becoming extinct. In countries like Thailand, which is home to the helmeted hornbill, people are now enacting special laws to help preserve the dwindling population of these intriguing birds. Hopefully, these laws will help hornbills to remain a source of wonder and amazement long into the future.

Unlike many of the octopus's relatives, such as snails and clams, octopuses do not have hard shells for protection. But their exceptional intelligence allows them to use their soft, boneless bodies to great advantage.

One way octopuses put the combined power of their brains and bodies to good use is by manipulating objects. Octopuses in Indonesia have been observed turning over, grasping, and carrying coconut shell halves, which they then assemble into a protective covering when needed. Other octopuses stack up rocks to block the entrances to their homes. This creative use of objects as tools is associated with very intelligent animals, including great apes such as chimpanzees and orangutans.

Octopuses are also the ultimate camouflage artists. They can hide themselves in plain sight, fooling both predators and prey. Within milliseconds, octopuses can adapt their skin to match their environment. One way they do this is by expanding and contracting little sacs of pigment in their skin. Small muscles pull different pigment sacs to the surface, changing the octopus's skin color. Octopuses also have papillae, small bumps on their skin, which they can squeeze, pull, and stretch into different sizes and shapes—from small, round bumps to tall spikes. By changing the texture of their skin, octopuses are able to blend in with objects around them, like coral and rocks, and avoid detection by predators.

Octopuses do not just change their skin to blend in with their surroundings; they also change the shape and motion of their bodies. They can curl, wave, or extend their tentacles to imitate things in their environment, like seaweed or algae. One species called mimic octopuses can even take on the appearance and movements of other sea animals like fish, sea snakes, and crabs. These shape-shifting octopuses mimic different species in different habitats and situations. For example, they can ward off predators by imitating the striped coloration, elongated shape, and swimming motion of a venomous fish called the banded sole. This suggests that they learn how to disguise themselves by observing their surroundings and judging their immediate needs.

Sometimes, the immediate need of an octopus might be to escape. In these situations, octopuses still have options. Their quick thinking and soft bodies make them true escape artists. They can squeeze themselves through the tiniest of cracks. They can also disappear into a cloud of toxic ink that they shoot out from a tube-shaped funnel called a siphon. They shoot water out of the siphon, too, to propel themselves through the water with surprising speed. And if a predator still manages to get hold of one of the octopus's tentacles, the octopus can sacrifice the arm, detaching it while jetting away. No need to worry: the tentacle will grow back, extra "brain" and all.

pieces.text: Tardigrades' unique characteristics and behaviors become evident when examined under a microscope. Scientists have nicknamed these miniature animals "water bears" and "moss piglets." Tardigrades have an almost cute appearance as they toddle around clumsily on their eight short legs. With sharp mouth parts called
, they pierce the cells of plants, algae, bacteria, and even other tiny animals. They suck up the liquid from the cells with straw-like tubes attached to their round mouths.

textContent.text: There are more than a thousand known species of tardigrades. They live everywhere on Earth, including in lakes, in deserts, and in the highest elevations of the tallest mountains. They can survive anyplace where even a small drop of water exists—like on a patch of moss. textContent.text: Somewhere along the line, spotted hyenas got a bad rap, and it stuck. They have been vilified in literature, African folktales, and modern movies as cowardly, evil scavengers that lie in wait to steal food from more noble hunters. But in reality, spotted hyenas are remarkably successful hunters that take down most of their own prey. Their food is more likely to be stolen by lions than the other way around. The more we learn about spotted hyenas, the more evident it becomes that they do not necessarily deserve their bad reputations.

Spotted hyenas have what many consider to be an odd appearance. They have coarse, yellowish coats covered in dark spots, with a shaggy mane of fur that sticks up along their backs. Like all hyena species, they have long, thick, muscular necks, and their front legs are longer than their back legs, giving them a sloped back. This body shape may look a little strange, but it also makes spotted hyenas powerful hunters. They can chase prey for miles at speeds of over thirty miles per hour. Their powerful jaws can crush bones; in fact, hyenas devour every part of an animal, including bones and skin. They leave nothing behind.

which sometimes include over one hundred individuals. Smaller groups within the clan work together to take down prey. But no matter who actually makes the kill, it is always the clan's top-ranking female and her pups that get to eat first. In fact, all adult females in a clan feed before adult males. This kind of social organization led by females is called a

. The top-ranking female passes on her high status to her offspring, both male and female. But when males reach the age of two or three, they leave the clan to find a mate. In their new clans, they are of the lowest rank.

textContent.text: For such a complex social structure to work, spotted hyenas need to be able to communicate with one another. The hyenas share information by relying on a set of at least eleven different vocalizations. The most famous is "laughing." But this giggling sound is not humorous; instead, the hyenas only laugh when they are in socially stressful situations. The hyena sound that people are actually most likely to hear is their whoop. Each spotted hyena has its own distinctive whoop that the others can recognize. In addition to laughing and whooping, spotted hyenas grunt, groan, and growl in different situations. They also use smells to mark their territories and body gestures to communicate with each other.

The ability to communicate helps hyenas live more effectively in groups. Understanding so many different sounds, scents, and gestures is no simple task, but hyenas are up for the challenge. According to researchers, spotted hyenas have problem-solving abilities similar to some of Earth's most intelligent animals, like chimpanzees. And the hyenas have another trait in common with chimps as well: they are great mothers. They raise their cubs together in communal dens, nursing them for up to eighteen months. The hyena mothers provide their cubs with the richest milk of any land carnivore. Perhaps this is part of the reason that spotted hyenas live so long. These hardy animals work together to survive, and people are starting to recognize that spotted hyenas are unexpectedly amazing.

textContent.text: Peccaries are often mistaken for pigs, as both are hoofed animals with thick necks, large heads, and long snouts. Unlike their pig cousins, however, peccaries have rounded, bear-like ears and small tails. While pigs have two lower teeth that curve out and back to form tusks, peccaries have small, straight tusks that are better for biting. To those unfamiliar with these creatures, peccaries can be a startling, almost comical sight. Their thick bodies are supported on twiggy legs, and they seem to walk "tippy-toe" on their delicate-looking hoofs. The most common species, the collared peccary, or javelina (pronounced ha-vah-LEE-nuh), has a light-colored "collar" that contrasts with the rest of its bristly brown hair.

Unlike pigs, which were brought from Europe, peccaries are native to the Americas. Herds, or squadrons, of collared peccaries are common sights in the desert regions of Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas. The peccaries' range also extends down through Mexico, Central America, and South America, where they can be found in diverse habitats, including grasslands and rainforests. The peccaries' diets vary depending on where they live. The animals often forage for leaves, roots, bulbs, nuts, and fruit. They also sometimes eat worms, eggs, and small reptiles. In North America, one of their favorite things to munch on is prickly pear cactus—spines and all!

Scientists have found that regardless of environment, peccaries are incredibly social animals. They live in large family groups and communicate with sounds like grunts, barks, and coughs. It can be entertaining to watch the playful young ones running, leaping, and chasing one another while the adults forage. But peccaries also make their presence known in another way: they can really stink! In fact, peccaries are sometimes called "skunk pigs" or "musk hogs." They mark their territories and identify other members of their family groups using a smelly substance that comes from special glands on their backs.

helps the peccaries keep cool in hot climates and remove parasites from their skin and hair. Plus, they seem to have a lot of fun doing it! But mud wallows do not only benefit the peccaries; they also play a surprisingly important role in the health of the overall ecosystems in which the animals live.

Over time, the wallows develop packed-down, claylike bottoms that hold water well. During the rainy season, the wallows collect water, forming little ponds; when the rainy season ends, these ponds stick around much longer than other seasonal water sources. The wallows are an important habitat for frogs and provide drinking water for many animals, like birds, bats, monkeys, pumas, and ocelots.

Peccaries help their ecosystems in another important way, too—by "gardening." Peccaries are messy eaters, leaving seeds strewn around on the ground and stuck on their fur. The seeds on the ground later sprout into new plants, while the seeds carried on the peccaries' fur are dropped farther away. When they sprout, the overall variety of plant life in the region is improved. As it turns out, peccaries are more important than their silly looks suggest. They are great neighbors, providing water, food, and a healthier habitat for their communities.

textContent.text: Peccaries are often mistaken for pigs, as both are hoofed animals with thick necks, large heads, and long snouts. Unlike their pig cousins, however, peccaries have rounded, bear-like ears and small tails. While pigs have two lower teeth that curve out and back to form tusks, peccaries have small, straight tusks that are better for biting. To those unfamiliar with these creatures, peccaries can be a startling, almost comical sight. Their thick bodies are supported on twiggy legs, and they seem to walk "tippy-toe" on their delicate-looking hoofs. The most common species, the collared peccary, or javelina (pronounced ha-vah-LEE-nuh), has a light-colored "collar" that contrasts with the rest of its bristly brown hair.

Unlike pigs, which were brought from Europe, peccaries are native to the Americas. Herds, or squadrons, of collared peccaries are common sights in the desert regions of Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas. The peccaries' range also extends down through Mexico, Central America, and South America, where they can be found in diverse habitats, including grasslands and rainforests. The peccaries' diets vary depending on where they live. The animals often forage for leaves, roots, bulbs, nuts, and fruit. They also sometimes eat worms, eggs, and small reptiles. In North America, one of their favorite things to munch on is prickly pear cactus—spines and all!

Scientists have found that regardless of environment, peccaries are incredibly social animals. They live in large family groups and communicate with sounds like grunts, barks, and coughs. It can be entertaining to watch the playful young ones running, leaping, and chasing one another while the adults forage. But peccaries also make their presence known in another way: they can really stink! In fact, peccaries are sometimes called "skunk pigs" or "musk hogs." They mark their territories and identify other members of their family groups using a smelly substance that comes from special glands on their backs.

pieces.text: Even though they smell bad, peccaries are generally clean animals. In addition to regularly grooming themselves and one another, they also take mud baths in water holes they create. Splashing and rolling in these

helps the peccaries keep cool in hot climates and remove parasites from their skin and hair. Plus, they seem to have a lot of fun doing it! But mud wallows do not only benefit the peccaries; they also play a surprisingly important role in the health of the overall ecosystems in which the animals live.

textContent.text: How can a mud wallow help maintain an ecosystem? Peccaries usually use the same wallows year after year. Over time, the wallows develop packed-down, claylike bottoms that hold water well. During the rainy season, the wallows collect water, forming little ponds; when the rainy season ends, these ponds stick around much longer than other seasonal water sources. The wallows are an important habitat for frogs and provide drinking water for many animals, like birds, bats, monkeys, pumas, and ocelots.

Peccaries help their ecosystems in another important way, too—by "gardening." Peccaries are messy eaters, leaving seeds strewn around on the ground and stuck on their fur. The seeds on the ground later sprout into new plants, while the seeds carried on the peccaries' fur are dropped farther away. When they sprout, the overall variety of plant life in the region is improved. As it turns out, peccaries are more important than their silly looks suggest. They are great neighbors, providing water, food, and a healthier habitat for their communities.
